prize_parts.citation: for the theory of the Z2 topological insulator and the quantum spin Hall state, and for its first experimental observation in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: Topological insulators remain, in my reading, the strongest case on the shortlist and the one most clearly a discovery in the sense of the statutes. The Z2 classification and the quantum spin Hall prediction established that protected boundary states follow from bulk band topology in time-reversal-invariant insulators, and the HgTe transport experiment showed the effect in a real material. Two decades of independent confirmation by transport, photoemission and scanning probes have made the interpretation stable. Seven of eight members ranked it, four placed it first and none below third among those who ranked it, which tells me the committee already sees a mature and broadly influential result. It is also a discovery with an unambiguous theory-plus-experiment structure, which is what the prize criterion of a discovery or invention asks for rather than a lifetime of good work.
statement.case_against: The attribution is the real weakness. The HgTe proposal by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang is not among the credited names, Zhang is deceased, and the three-dimensional theory and experiments (Fu, Kane, Mele, Moore, Balents, Hsieh, Hasan) cannot all be honoured under a three-person cap. Whichever trio we choose leaves out someone with a substantial claim. There is also a fair argument that the 2016 prize for topological phases already covers this territory, and that the committee would be rewarding a second topological prize while other fields wait.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B006 first but proposes Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan, and says leaving out Mele and the HgTe proposers is a real fairness problem; he also flags unsettled priority for the first 3D observation.
responses.response: I made the same proposal in my opening and I agree with the fairness concern, which is why I have moved. The Kane-Mele papers are a joint work and I cannot give a principled reason for crediting one author and not the other. Hasan's ARPES work is important for the 3D materials, and as a microscopist and spectroscopist I value it, but the prize must name the discovery. The quantum spin Hall prediction and its observation is the cleaner, singly attributable discovery, and the 3D priority dispute you note (Bi-Sb, Bi2Se3, and the theory preceding it) makes that part harder to defend as a settled three-name credit. I would rather the citation be defensible on the 2D discovery than broad and contested.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B017 first, as a clear theory-prediction followed by experiment in a tunable platform, and ranks B006 second, noting that recognition of the Z2 insulators is if anything overdue even after the 2016 prize.
responses.response: I accept your argument on the 2016 overlap: that prize covered topological phase transitions and the integer quantum Hall and Haldane story, whereas the Z2 insulators are a distinct discovery with a distinct experimental signature. On B017 I agree the prediction-to-experiment link is elegant, and I ranked it second myself. Where we differ is maturity. The pairing mechanism is open and the phase diagram is still moving, and the prize would rest on observing correlated and superconducting phases rather than on an explanation. That is acceptable in principle, but I would put it after B006 on timing. I also note your concern about Yuan Cao and experimental credit, which I share and which weighs against a clean three-name prize.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube (B048) second as a bold instrument delivering a new window on the Universe, while acknowledging his own background as a possible bias and the difficulty of crediting a very large collaboration with two names.
responses.response: I ranked B048 eighth and I want to be fair to it: the diffuse flux is a real discovery and the instrument is remarkable. My reservation is attribution and maturity of the physics, not importance. A prize needs to identify the people responsible for the original work, and IceCube's result rests on a collaboration of hundreds plus AMANDA and Baikal predecessors, so naming Halzen and Karle alone compresses credit more than any other ballot here. The source identifications (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068) are still statistically modest. I would keep it as a strong later candidate rather than a 2026 prize.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the optical lattice clock (B047) first, as a clear and original advance with consequences for timekeeping, geodesy and constants, with a natural two-person share, and notes the pending SI redefinition of the second.
responses.response: I agree this is an invention with a clean two-name credit and I ranked it third, so I would not oppose it. My question to you and to Kroll is whether it is distinct enough from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes. I think it is: the magic-wavelength trapping is a genuinely new idea and the 1e-18 regime is its own result. I do not think we need to wait for the formal redefinition of the second; the discovery does not depend on it. Where I differ is only in ordering, because B006 has the broader scientific consequence across several subfields, whereas B047 is concentrated in metrology.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED (B038) first as a conceptually clean transfer of cavity QED to superconducting circuits that underlies most processors, and argues it is distinct from the 2025 prize.
responses.response: I agree the concept is clean and the architecture is widely used, and I ranked it fourth. My reservation is timing and kind: coming one year after the prize for macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits, a second award to the same community invites the charge of repetition, and cQED is closer to an enabling architecture than a new phenomenon of nature. I also note that Girvin's omission from the 2004 proposal credit is a real attribution gap. I am open to being persuaded that the distinction from the 2025 prize is strong enough, but I would want the committee to say so explicitly.

uncertainties: Whether the committee can fairly exclude Zhang's, Bernevig's and Hughes's HgTe proposal and the 3D topological insulator discoverers, including Hasan, under a three-person cap.
Whether the 2016 prize for topological phases is judged to reduce room for a topological insulator prize.
Whether the optical lattice clock is distinct enough from the 2005 and 2012 metrology prizes to outrank B006 for some members.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for the shortlisted candidates. I share an institution (Chalmers) with Göran Johansson, who ranks circuit QED first, and I have long-standing Japanese academic exchanges and the microscopy federation role, but none of these is documented as a connection to the credited names on the shortlist.
